title: SAA-C03 Domain 1 — Blast Radius
description: The second half of the security domain: public and private subnets, the two firewall objects everyone confuses, endpoints, and encryption at rest and in transit.

lines.text: A company does the responsible thing. It moves every workload out of public subnets and into private ones.
Good. That is the advice everyone gives.
It is. And the next month the bill goes up, in a line item nobody was watching. Data processing charges on a NAT gateway.
From what? The instances are private now. They are barely talking to the internet.
They are talking to S3. And S3 sits outside the private network, so every byte was being pulled through the NAT gateway and charged by the gigabyte.
There is an object that fixes this, it costs nothing to run, and it is one route table entry. It also happens to be a security control. That is where we finish today.

sections.title: The other half of domain one

lines.text: Domain one, second half. Task one point two, secure workloads and applications. Task one point three, data security controls.
Last time was who is allowed to do what. This is where they are allowed to do it from.
And what state the data is in while they do it. Here is the question for this episode. What is the smallest change that reduces the blast radius the most?
The exam actually asks it that way?
It asks it as most secure, or least exposure, or meets the compliance requirement. Same question underneath. And several answers will all be technically secure.
Start with the pair that gets confused more than any other on this exam. Security groups and network access control lists.
A security group attaches to a network interface, so effectively to an instance. A network access control list attaches to a subnet, so it covers everything in that subnet.
So one is per machine, one is per neighbourhood.

That is the right picture. Now the difference that decides the questions. A security group is stateful. If you allow traffic in, the reply is allowed out automatically. You never write the return rule.

A network access control list is stateless. It has no memory of the request. So the reply is evaluated on its own, against the outbound rules, and if you forgot the ephemeral port range the reply is dropped.
That is the classic broken connection where the request arrives and the answer never comes back.
That is the classic. And here is the second difference. A security group can only allow. There is no deny rule in one. A network access control list has both allow and deny.

So if a question needs one specific address blocked while everything else stays open, it cannot be a security group. That is a network access control list, because blocking is the only thing the other one cannot do.
Now subnets. There is no checkbox that makes a subnet public. A subnet is public because its route table sends internet-bound traffic to an internet gateway. That is the whole definition.
So a private subnet is just one without that route.
Exactly, and that is why the NAT gateway exists. It sits in a public subnet and lets private instances reach out, while nothing on the internet can reach in. Outbound only, by design.
Which brings us to the object from the cold open. A VPC endpoint. It lets resources inside your network reach an AWS service without the traffic leaving the AWS network at all.
There are two kinds and the exam tests the split. A gateway endpoint serves S3 and DynamoDB, it is a route table entry, and there is no hourly charge and no data processing charge.
An interface endpoint serves almost everything else. It is a network interface with a private address inside your subnet, and it does carry an hourly charge and a data charge.
So the free one covers the two services everybody uses most.
Which is why the cold open is a real bill and not a story. S3 traffic through a NAT gateway is a charge you did not need to pay.
Now data. A compliance requirement lands. All data at rest must be encrypted, and the company must control the key material and be able to rotate it.
Then we manage our own keys. Generate them ourselves, keep them off AWS, and hand them over per request. It says the company must control the key.
You have described customer provided keys, and it is a defensible reading. Tell me what you have just signed up for operationally.
Storing the key somewhere. Supplying it on every single request. And if we lose it, the data is gone.

All of that, and no audit trail of key use, and no rotation without re-encrypting everything by hand. Now read the requirement again. It says control and rotate. It does not say hold the bytes yourself.
So a customer managed key in the Key Management Service.

That is the answer the exam wants, and here is why. A customer managed key has a key policy you write, so you control who may use it. It logs every use to CloudTrail, so you can prove it. And it rotates on a schedule you set.

Compare that with the default. Server side encryption with keys the service manages is one checkbox and it is genuinely encrypted, but you do not get a key policy and you cannot deny a specific team access to the key.
So the discriminator is not whether it is encrypted. Both are.
The discriminator is who holds the authority over the key, and whether you need to prove it. Words like audit, control, rotate, or separate duties all point at a customer managed key.

Data in transit is the easier half. Certificate Manager issues and renews the certificate, and it attaches to a load balancer, a distribution or an API. Public certificates from it are free, and renewal is automatic.
So any answer about an expiring certificate and a manual renewal process is the wrong one.
Almost always. If the pain in the question is a certificate that expired and took the site down, the fix in the answer is the managed service that renews it for you.

sections.title: Network and data in one pass

lines.text: One pass. Nothing new in here.

A security group sits on an instance, is stateful, and can only allow. A network access control list sits on a subnet, is stateless, and can also deny. If a question needs one address blocked, it is the list.
A subnet is public only because its route table points at an internet gateway. A NAT gateway lets private instances reach outward without letting anything reach in.

A VPC endpoint keeps traffic to AWS services off the public path entirely. Gateway endpoints cover S3 and DynamoDB and are free. Interface endpoints cover the rest and are charged by the hour and by the gigabyte.

At rest, encryption is the easy part and the key policy is the answer. A customer managed key when the requirement mentions control, audit, rotation, or separation of duties. In transit, Certificate Manager, issued and renewed for you.
And the bill from the cold open.
One gateway endpoint. No hourly charge, no data charge, and the traffic never leaves the AWS network. More secure and cheaper at the same time, which is rarer than it sounds.
Drill. Question one. A request reaches an instance and the reply never arrives. Which of the two firewall objects is the likely cause, and why?
The network access control list. It is stateless, so the reply is checked against the outbound rules, and the ephemeral port range is probably missing.
Question two. You must block one specific address and leave everything else open. Which object, and why not the other one?
The network access control list, because a security group has no deny rule at all.
Question three. What actually makes a subnet public?
A route in its route table sending internet-bound traffic to an internet gateway. Nothing else.
Question four. Private instances read heavily from S3 and the NAT gateway charges are high. Cheapest fix?
A gateway endpoint for S3. It is a route table entry, and there is no hourly or data processing charge.
Three traps and their mechanisms.

Trap one is the security service line-up. Four names appear together and only one matches. Shield is for denial of service attacks. Web Application Firewall is for request level attacks like injection.
GuardDuty detects suspicious activity from logs. Macie finds sensitive data sitting in S3. Detection is not prevention, and the question will tell you which one it wants.
And the tell?
The verb. Block and protect point at Shield or the Web Application Firewall. Discover, identify and alert point at GuardDuty or Macie. If the sensitive data is in a bucket, it is Macie.
Trap two is secrets. Secrets Manager rotates credentials automatically and charges per secret. Parameter Store holds configuration securely and is cheaper, but does not rotate on its own.

If the question says automatic rotation of a database password, it is Secrets Manager. If it says store configuration at low cost, it is Parameter Store. And an answer that puts a credential in an environment variable is never right.

Trap three is the private connection pair. A site to site virtual private network runs over the public internet and is encrypted. Direct Connect is a dedicated private link, and it is not encrypted by itself.
So consistent performance points at Direct Connect, and encryption points at the virtual private network.
And a question that demands both is asking you to run the virtual private network over Direct Connect. That combination is a real answer option, and people skip past it.
Three questions for yourself.
One. Stateful or stateless. Which of the two firewall objects makes you write the return rule yourself?
Two. What single thing makes a subnet public?
Three. Which words in a requirement force you off the default encryption and onto a customer managed key?
Control, audit, rotate, separate duties.
Those four. And that closes domain one, the thirty percent, across two episodes.

sections.title: Marks per hour, and next time

lines.text: Marks per hour: high, and it pays twice. The endpoint that fixed the bill in the cold open is a cost optimisation answer as well as a security one.
Next time, domain two. Design resilient architectures, twenty six percent, and the question underneath all of it. How much are you willing to lose, and how long are you willing to be down.
